name: MathlibAnnex.BilipschitzOrientation.signed_area_transfer
title: Signed transfer from the absolute Jacobian formula

content.display_title: Signed transfer from the absolute Jacobian formula
content.one_sentence_role: Transfers an integrable function without first assuming that the Jacobian sign is constant.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $E=\mathbb R^n$ have the sup norm $\|\cdot\|_\infty$. Let $S,T\subseteq E$ be open, and let $f,g:E\to E$ be globally Lipschitz maps whose restrictions $f|_S:S\to T$ and $g|_T:T\to S$ are mutually inverse. Fix a number $\ell>0$ such that
$$\ell\|x-x'\|_\infty\le\|f(x)-f(x')\|_\infty\qquad(x,x'\in E).$$

Write $Df(x):E\to E$ for the Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$ when it exists, and set $Df(x)=0$ at other points. Define the signed Jacobian by $J_f(x)=\det Df(x)$.

Define the source sign $s_f:E\to\{-1,1\}$ and its transport $\sigma_f:E\to\{-1,1\}$ by
$$s_f(x)=\begin{cases}1,&J_f(x)\ge0,\\-1,&J_f(x)<0,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_f(y)=s_f(g(y)).$$
In particular, a zero determinant gives sign $+1$, and $|\sigma_f(y)|=1$ for every $y$.

All integrals use Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on these fixed coordinates. Let $\phi:E\to\mathbb R$ be integrable on $T$. Then
$$\int_S\phi(f(x))J_f(x)\,d\lambda(x)=\int_T\phi(y)\sigma_f(y)\,d\lambda(y).$$
content.assumptions:
The integrability hypothesis is $\phi\in L^1(T,\lambda)$. No connectedness assumption is made on $S$ or $T$.

The sets $S,T\subseteq E$ are open. The inverse and image conditions are
$$\begin{aligned}
f(S)&\subseteq T,&g(T)&\subseteq S,\\
g(f(x))&=x\quad(x\in S),&f(g(y))&=y\quad(y\in T).
\end{aligned}$$
The global bounds use specified constants $C_f,C_g\ge0$ and $\ell>0$:
$$\ell\|x-x'\|_\infty\le\|f(x)-f(x')\|_\infty\le C_f\|x-x'\|_\infty\qquad(x,x'\in E),$$
$$\|g(y)-g(y')\|_\infty\le C_g\|y-y'\|_\infty\qquad(y,y'\in E).$$
The estimates hold on all of $E$, not just on $S$ or $T$. The inverse identities are required only on $S$ and $T$.
content.conclusion: The factor on the target is the sign of the source Jacobian evaluated at the inverse point $g(y)$. It may vary with $y$. Both integrands are integrable on their respective sets.
content.proof_summary: Discard a null subset of $S$ and a null subset of $T$, apply the injective absolute area formula, and use $g(f(x))=x$ to restore the signed determinant.

proof_steps.text:
**Identify the two null complements.** Define
$$N=\{x\in E:f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\},\qquad G=S\setminus N.$$
Then
$$\lambda(N)=0,\qquad \lambda(S\setminus G)=0,\qquad \lambda(f(N))=0.$$
The first equality is [Rademacher's theorem](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/Rademacher.lean#L387-L390) for the globally Lipschitz map $f$ on the finite-dimensional space $E$. The second follows from $S\setminus G\subseteq N$. The third is [preservation of null sets by an equal-dimensional Lipschitz map](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Basic.lean#L80-L97), with this same $f$ and $N$; it is also recorded by [the target-exception lemma](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Basic.lean#L199-L203). The set $G$ is measurable because $S$ and the differentiability set are measurable.

The inverse identities give
$$f(G)\subseteq T,\qquad T\setminus f(G)\subseteq f(N),\qquad \lambda(T\setminus f(G))=0.$$
Indeed, if $y\in T\setminus f(G)$, then $g(y)\in S$ and $f(g(y))=y$. Hence $g(y)\notin G$, so $g(y)\in N$ and $y\in f(N)$.

**Apply the absolute formula to the signed function.** Put $\psi(y)=\phi(y)\sigma_f(y)$. The sign $\sigma_f$ is measurable and $|\psi|=|\phi|$, so $\psi$ is integrable on $T$ and on $f(G)$. The formula to be used is
$$\int_{f(G)}\psi(y)\,d\lambda(y)=\int_G |J_f(x)|\psi(f(x))\,d\lambda(x).$$
For [the injective absolute Jacobian formula](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/Jacobian.lean#L1214-L1227), the domain is the measurable set $G$, the map is $f$, the derivative at each $x\in G$ is $Df(x)$ (also a derivative within $G$), and the measure is $\lambda$. Injectivity on $G$ follows from $g(f(x))=x$ on $S$. With these same inputs, [the corresponding integrability equivalence](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/Jacobian.lean#L1203-L1212) gives integrability of the right-hand integrand.

**Substitute the inverse and remove the null complements.** For $x\in G$,
$$\sigma_f(f(x))=s_f(g(f(x)))=s_f(x),\qquad s_f(x)|J_f(x)|=J_f(x).$$
The second identity is [the signed determinant identity](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Calculus/BilipschitzOrientation/Basic.lean#L181-L197) at this differentiability point. Therefore
$$|J_f(x)|\psi(f(x))=|J_f(x)|\phi(f(x))\sigma_f(f(x))=\phi(f(x))J_f(x).$$
Substituting this equality into Step 2 and using the null complements from Step 1 gives
$$\begin{aligned}
\int_S\phi(f(x))J_f(x)\,d\lambda(x)
&=\int_G\phi(f(x))J_f(x)\,d\lambda(x)\\
&=\int_{f(G)}\phi(y)\sigma_f(y)\,d\lambda(y)\\
&=\int_T\phi(y)\sigma_f(y)\,d\lambda(y).
\end{aligned}$$
The first and last replacements are justified by $\lambda(S\setminus G)=0$ and $\lambda(T\setminus f(G))=0$, respectively. The source integrability obtained in Step 2 is preserved by the first replacement.

content.lean_realization_notes: The total derivative is measurable, its determinant is measurable, and the displayed two-valued sign is measurable. Since $g$ is continuous, $\sigma_f=s_f\circ g$ is measurable as well. These facts justify the integrability assertion for $\phi\sigma_f$ used in the proof. The two global Lipschitz constants are exactly those supplied for $f$ and $g$ in the assumptions.
